title: The Brus
description: John Barbour's verse chronicle of Robert Bruce and the Scottish wars of independence, completed c. 1375 in some 14,000 octosyllabic lines: the murder of the Red Comyn, the crowning at Scone, the years of guerrilla warfare, and the great victory at Bannockburn (1314), with James Douglas as the poem's second hero. The first great work of Scottish literature and the fountainhead of the nation's heroic self-image.
plot_or_argument: The poem follows Bruce from the killing of Comyn and his coronation through defeat, exile, and the legendary perseverance of the spider episode to the recovery of the kingdom castle by castle, the battle of Bannockburn, the raids of Douglas into England, and the king's death — all framed by the poem's great theme, that 'fredome is a noble thing'.
narrative_structure: Twenty books of continuous narrative in the romance-chronicle manner, with set-piece battles and speeches, closed by the king's death and the poet's envoy.
principal_characters: Robert Bruce; James Douglas; Edward II; Edward Bruce; the Scottish and English armies
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets of energy and speed, in Older Scots.
historical_context: Completed in 1375 by the archdeacon of Aberdeen, in the court of Robert II (Bruce's grandson), when the Stewart dynasty needed a heroic past; preserved in two manuscripts (1487, 1489) and printed in 1571.
literary_significance: The first great poem in Scots and the founding text of Scottish national literature; Burns's 'Scots Wha Hae' and the whole Bruce tradition descend from it.
attribution_notes: Barbour's authorship secure (named in the text and the royal records).
bibliographical_notes: St John's College, Cambridge, MS G.23 (1487). Standard edition: M. P. McDiarmid and J. A. C. Stevenson, STS, 3 vols (1980–85).

title: The Wallace
alternative_titles: The Acts and Deeds of Sir William Wallace
description: Blind Hary's epic life of William Wallace, composed c. 1477 in some 11,800 lines: the hero's outlawry after the killing of Selkirk's sheriff, his battles against the English — Stirling Bridge, the invasion of England, Falkirk — his betrayal and execution at London (1305), and his posthumous vindication. For four centuries it was, after the Bible, the most read book in Scotland, and it fixed Wallace in the national memory.
plot_or_argument: Wallace, driven to outlawry by English oppression, gathers his men, defeats the English at Stirling Bridge, harries England as far as York, and is named guardian of Scotland; betrayed at Falkirk and by the treachery of Menteith, he is taken to London, tried as a traitor to a king he never acknowledged, and executed — his dismembered body displayed, his fame immortal.
narrative_structure: Twelve books of epic narrative, from outlawry through triumph to martyrdom, in the minstrel chronicle manner, with the poet's appeals to his audience throughout.
principal_characters: William Wallace; Edward I; Menteith; Graham; Bruce (epilogue)
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets in Older Scots, declamatory and rapid.
historical_context: Composed c. 1477 by Blind Hary, who recited it before James IV for payment, drawing on John Blair's lost Latin life and oral tradition; printed by Chepman and Myllar (c. 1508) and endlessly reprinted — Burns acknowledged it as his first poetic inspiration.
literary_significance: The great popular epic of Scotland: its Wallace shaped the national hero for five centuries, and its influence on Burns and the romantic revival of Scottish identity is incalculable.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Blind Hary (Henry the Minstrel) by the poem and the treasurer's accounts.
bibliographical_notes: National Library of Scotland, Advocates' MS 19.2.2 (1488). Standard edition: M. P. McDiarmid, STS, 2 vols (1968–69).

title: The Kingis Quair
description: The dream vision traditionally attributed to James I of Scotland, written c. 1424 after his eighteen years of captivity in England: the imprisoned narrator, sleepless with love, reads Boethius, sees his lady from the tower window, and is taught by the goddesses of Love, Fortune, and Wisdom in a vision that reconciles him to his fate. The fountainhead of the Scottish Chaucerian tradition.
plot_or_argument: The sleepless captive, turning the pages of Boethius, hears the bell of matins and falls into a dream; guided by the goddesses, he ascends to the sphere of Venus, where his love for the lady seen from the tower is confirmed and fortune's wheel is explained; waking, a dove brings him the message of hope, and he ends his book in praise of love and his lady.
narrative_structure: A single dream vision in the Chaucerian-Boethian manner: reading, waking complaint, dream ascent, counsel of the goddesses, and waking resolution.
principal_characters: the captive narrator (James I); the lady (Joan Beaufort); Venus; Minerva; Fortune; the dove
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal stanzas of Chaucerian fluency, in Older Scots.
historical_context: Composed c. 1424, on the eve of James's release, celebrating his love for Joan Beaufort, whom he married in February 1424; preserved uniquely in the Selden manuscript (Bodleian Arch. Selden. B.24, c. 1488).
literary_significance: The fountainhead of the makars' tradition: the first great poem in the Scottish Chaucerian line and the model for the royal and courtly poetry of the Stewart century.
attribution_notes: The attribution to James I rests on the poem's autobiographical frame and manuscript tradition; it is widely but not universally accepted.
bibliographical_notes: Bodleian Library, MS Arch. Selden. B.24. Standard edition: L. R. Mooney and M.-J. Arn, TEAMS (2005).

title: The Morall Fabillis of Esope the Phrygian
description: Robert Henryson's cycle of thirteen beast fables (c. 1480s), translating and transforming Aesopian material into the great vernacular fable collection of the British Middle Ages: the cock and the jasper, the two mice, the lion and the mouse, the fox and the wolf, and the parliament of beasts before King Lion. Its moralitates raise the fable to satiric and philosophical art, with a marked sympathy for the poor and the small.
plot_or_argument: The fables move from the country mouse's visit to the town and back, through the fox's adventures with the wolf and the cock's with the fox, to the lion's parliament, where the beasts' complaints against their rulers and their own natures are heard and judged; each fable closes with its moralitas applying the tale to the estates of men.
narrative_structure: A prologue and thirteen fables, each bipartite (taill and moralitas), in the medieval Aesopic tradition raised to a coherent cycle.
principal_characters: the Cock and the Fox; the Town and Country Mice; the Lion; the Wolf; the Sheep; the Swallow; the Toad
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal stanzas of supple, colloquial power in Older Scots.
historical_context: Composed c. 1480s by the Dunfermline schoolmaster Robert Henryson, in the European fable revival of the fifteenth century (Steinhöwel, Caxton's Aesop of 1484); printed in 1570–71, and preserved in the Bannatyne and other manuscripts.
literary_significance: The summit of the medieval European fable tradition in any vernacular: its moralitates are among the finest medieval poems on justice, poverty, and power.
attribution_notes: Henryson's authorship secure (named in the manuscripts).
bibliographical_notes: Bannatyne MS; Charteris print (1570). Standard edition: D. Fox, The Poems of Robert Henryson (1981).

title: The Testament of Cresseid
description: Robert Henryson's great continuation of Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde (616 lines, c. 1475–90): the abandoned Cresseid, stricken with leprosy as judgement on her blasphemy against Venus and Cupid, meets the leper troop at the roadside and is recognized, too late, by Troilus, who cannot name her but casts her alms; she dies repentant, her testament a warning against the falsehood of love and fortune. The most powerful 'continuation' in English literature.
plot_or_argument: The narrator, taking up 'ane uther quair' on the fate of Cresseid, tells how Diomede abandoned her; in her complaint she blasphemes Venus and Cupid, and the planetary court, convened by Saturn and Cynthia, condemns her to leprosy; in the lazar house she meets Troilus, who pities the unknown leper; learning the truth from the leper woman, she makes her testament, dies, and is buried under a tomb inscribed with her tragedy.
narrative_structure: A five-movement tragedy (abandonment; blasphemy and judgement; leprosy; the roadside meeting; testament and death), closed by the narrator's warning to the women of the audience.
principal_characters: Cresseid; Troilus; Diomede; Saturn; Cynthia; Venus; Cupid; the leper woman
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal stanzas of austere, compassionate power in Older Scots.
historical_context: Composed c. 1475–90 in the Chaucerian tradition of the Scottish makars, answering Chaucer's Troilus with a Scottish judgement on its heroine; printed with Chaucer's works by Thynne (1532), where it long passed as Chaucer's own.
literary_significance: Universally ranked among the great short tragedies of English literature; its compassion for Cresseid and its cosmic judgement scene make it the supreme Scottish response to Chaucer.
attribution_notes: Henryson's authorship secure (named in the manuscripts).
bibliographical_notes: BL Harley MS 3865, etc.; Thynne's 1532 Chaucer. Standard edition: D. Fox, The Poems of Robert Henryson (1981).

title: Orpheus and Eurydice
description: Robert Henryson's retelling of the Orpheus myth (c. 1480, 633 lines): the harper-king's descent to the underworld to reclaim Eurydice, his fatal backward look, and — in Henryson's distinctive addition — a long moralitas allegorizing Orpheus as the intellect, Eurydice as the appetite, and the harrowing journey as the soul's quest for its lost harmony. The most learned of the makars' classical poems.
plot_or_argument: Orpheus, whose harping masters the beasts and the spheres, loses Eurydice to the serpent's bite and follows her to the underworld, where his music wins her release on the one condition; his backward look loses her forever, and the poet's moralitas expounds the fable as the story of reason seeking the soul's lost good.
narrative_structure: A bipartite poem: the classical narrative (with its celebrated catalogue of the underworld's inhabitants) followed by the allegorical moralitas.
principal_characters: Orpheus; Eurydice; Pluto; Proserpina; the Furies; the narrator
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal stanzas, with the moralitas in Henryson's plainest expository verse.
historical_context: Composed c. 1480, drawing on Boethius's Consolation (the standard medieval source for the myth) and the commentary tradition; printed by Chepman and Myllar (1508), the first printed Scots poem.
literary_significance: The classic Scottish treatment of the Orpheus myth and a landmark in the allegorical reading of classical poetry that runs from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance.
bibliographical_notes: Chepman and Myllar print (1508). Standard edition: D. Fox, The Poems of Robert Henryson (1981).

title: The Tretis of the Tua Mariit Wemen and the Wedo
alternative_titles: The Treatise of the Two Married Women and the Widow
description: William Dunbar's scandalous Midsummer Eve debate (c. 1500–07, 530 lines): the eavesdropping poet overhears three women — two wives and a widow — exchanging frank confidences on marriage, their husbands' inadequacies, and the arts of deceiving them, in the most sustained exhibition of female licence (and male ventriloquism) in medieval English verse. The most brilliant of Dunbar's alliterative poems.
plot_or_argument: Hidden in the hedge on a June night, the narrator hears the first wife anatomize her husband's age, impotence, and jealousy, the second mock hers as a coward and braggart, and the widow — dismissing both as amateurs — advise on choosing, managing, and surviving husbands, until the dawn and the lark's song end the colloquy.
narrative_structure: A debate-frame of three long monologues, each more outrageous than the last, in the tradition of the débat and the Wife of Bath's prologue.
principal_characters: the narrator (Dunbar); the two married women; the widow
meter_and_prosody: The unrhymed alliterative long line in Dunbar's hands — colloquial, obscene, and metrically audacious.
historical_context: Composed c. 1500–07 at the court of James IV, in the makars' revival of alliterative verse; printed by Chepman and Myllar (1508) and preserved in the Bannatyne manuscript.
literary_significance: The supreme comic-satiric poem of the Scottish tradition: its frankness and metrical brilliance made it a scandal in its own day and a touchstone of medieval misogyny debate in ours.
bibliographical_notes: Chepman and Myllar print (1508); Bannatyne MS. Standard edition: P. Bawcutt, The Poems of William Dunbar (1998).

title: Lament for the Makaris
description: William Dunbar's elegy on the poets ('makaris') of Scotland and the world (c. 1505, 100 lines): a procession of the dead — Chaucer, Lydgate, Gower, Henryson, and the court poets of the Stewart kings — each stanza closed by the refrain 'Timor mortis conturbat me' (the fear of death troubles me). The greatest short elegy of the Scottish tradition, and the poem that gave the makars their name.
plot_or_argument: The poet, reflecting that all things must die, calls the roll of the dead poets: first the great English trio of Chaucer, Gower, and Lydgate, then the Scottish makers — Barbour, Hary, Holland, and above all 'the noble rhetor' Henryson — and finally the court poets of his own youth, closing with the fear of death and the petition that God provide for the poet before he joins them.
narrative_structure: Twenty-five stanzas of single-movement elegy, the refrain tolling each catalogue entry, in the ubi sunt tradition.
principal_characters: Dunbar (speaker); the dead poets (Chaucer, Gower, Lydgate, Barbour, Hary, Henryson, and others)
meter_and_prosody: Four-line stanzas with the Latin refrain, austere and musical.
historical_context: Composed c. 1505 at the court of James IV, when Dunbar's generation was passing and the print era beginning; printed by Chepman and Myllar (1508); it names the Scottish tradition 'makaris' for all later criticism.
literary_significance: One of the great elegies in the language: its roll-call fixed the canon of the makars and its refrain became the proverbial voice of late medieval mortality.
bibliographical_notes: Chepman and Myllar print (1508); Bannatyne MS. Standard edition: P. Bawcutt, The Poems of William Dunbar (1998).
